what_it_does: When chip designers modify a circuit's arithmetic logic — say, changing how two numbers are multiplied — they need to prove that the new version still computes exactly the same outputs as the original. This process is called combinational equivalence checking (CEC): you compare two circuits, input by input, to confirm they agree everywhere. For complex arithmetic circuits this verification problem can become enormous and slow, and existing software tools often time out or give up. This paper describes a method called Parallel Dynamic Partitioning (PDP-CEC) that splits the big verification problem at carefully chosen internal nodes into many smaller, independent sub-problems that can be checked simultaneously across multiple processor cores. A dynamic task scheduler ensures that the work is spread evenly so no single hard sub-problem creates a bottleneck that stalls everything else. The approach is intended to make formal verification of large arithmetic chip designs both faster and more reliable.
